newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia hopes to join CEFTA by mid '98.
newsitem.headline: Croatia hopes to join CEFTA by mid '98.

text.p: Croatia plans to intensify talks in 1997 to join world and regional trade organisations, including the Central European Free Trade Agreement (CEFTA), diplomatic and economic sources said on Thursday.

"Achieving full membership in CEFTA, which can realistically be expected by mid-1998, is Croatia's top priority in foreign policy at the moment," said a Foreign Ministry official, speaking on condition of anonymity.
"We are also expecting and hoping to join the World Trade Organisation (WTO) and reach a cooperation agreement with the European Union by the end of the year."
A draft cooperation deal with the EU was prepared for ratification in 1995, but a Croatian Army offensive to retake the key Serb-held region of Krajina put it off indefinitely.
"The EU now wants to 'start' negotiations about the cooperation agreement and we want to 'continue' them, but contacts will resume by the end of February," the official said.
Croatia's long-term interest lies in joining the EU, which accounts for 60 percent of its foreign trade, but diplomats realise this is a long shot settle for a more realistic goal in the near future.
"We might become an EU member in 10-15 years, but our immediate goal is to join CEFTA," the official said.

In order take part in the free trade zone with a population of 70 million, Croatia first has to complete talks with the WTO and then negotiate with Poland, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Hungary and Slovenia.
The agreement went into effect in February 1993 and the former Yugolsav republic of Slovenia joined it in 1995.
Intensive negotiations with the Czech Republic and Slovakia have already begun, while contacts with others have been initiated.
Croatia's Adriatic port of Rijeka is an obvious trade outlet for Hungary, the Czech Republic and Slovakia, none of which have their own access to the sea.

Croatian conomics sources said its exports could suffer if the country lagged behind Slovenia, its third foreign trade partner after Germany and Italy, in joining CEFTA and achieving associate membership of the EU.
"Foreign trade currents have been diverted from Croatia because we are late in joining CEFTA," said Biserka Paukovic of the Croatian Chamber of Commerce.
